body: Mathematician who proved blackjack card counting (Beat the Dealer, 1962) and then applied the same logic to markets: only bet when you can quantify a positive expectation, and size by the Kelly criterion. Princeton Newport Partners (Nov 1969-1988): ~19.1% gross / ~15.1% net annualised (some sources say 20% net), with one source reporting 227 winning months and 3 losing months (all <1%). Structural edge: early mathematical pricing of warrants and options (a Black-Scholes-like formula before 1973), convertible arbitrage, statistical arbitrage - hedged, market-neutral books. The fund closed after the 1988 RICO raid tied to the Drexel investigation; Thorp was never charged. He also spotted Madoff in 1991 by noticing the options volume Madoff claimed to trade did not exist. Mistake: the partnership's structural dependence on a partner's office (the RICO case) ended a great record - operational/counterparty risk, not market risk. Copyable for individuals: (1) half-Kelly or smaller sizing - never bet so big that a loss ends the game; (2) check feasibility of any too-smooth record before trusting it; (3) Thorp himself recommends index funds for most people. Not copyable: arbitrage infrastructure.

data.copyable: fractional Kelly, fraud feasibility checks, indexing

title: Ed Thorp - quantified edge and Kelly sizing

body: Managed HDFC Equity (from Zurich India days, ~1994) and HDFC Top 100 until July 2022 (~28 years). HDFC Equity: ~19.3% CAGR since launch and beat its benchmark in 18 of 21 years; ~20% 20-year CAGR vs ~9.7% for the Nifty (Outlook). Process: valuation discipline, low turnover, willingness to look wrong for years; avoided the 2000 tech bubble and the 2007 realty mania at peak multiples, and leaned into unloved large caps (PSU banks, power, oil, capital goods). His line: 'If there is no pain, why should valuations be attractive?' Structural edge: very large AUM in an era when Indian MF competition was thin; later, size became a constraint (Business Standard 2013). Biggest mistake: 2018-2020 underperformance from an outsized bet on PSUs (SBI, NTPC, Coal India, BPCL etc.) whose value did not turn into growth, causing heavy redemptions and Morningstar downgrades; the PSU bets finally paid off in the last ~18 months of his HDFC stint. Founded 3P Investment Managers (May 2023), >Rs 15,000 crore AUM in two funds. Copyable: valuation discipline in large caps and the stamina to hold an underweight in bubbles; but recognise that cheap PSUs can stay cheap for years without a catalyst (capex cycle, NPA clean-up).

data.copyable: valuation discipline, patience, avoid bubble multiples

title: Prashant Jain - valuation-disciplined large-cap contrarian (India)

body: Flag: MOSTLY-CLEAN. Chandrakant Birla's group (an older branch of the Birla family). Listed: Orient Electric, HIL (Birla Aerocon, roofing), Birlasoft, Orient Paper & Industries, and formerly Orient Cement. Orient Cement sale (Oct-2024): Ambuja Cements (Adani) agreed to buy 46.8% at Rs 395.40/share (~Rs 8,100 cr, ~12% premium to prior close), triggering a mandatory 26% open offer to public shareholders at the same price; the letter of offer was delayed to May-2025 pending approvals -- minorities received the same price as promoters (good conduct). No regulator enforcement findings against the group were found in this scan; group companies are mid-caps with moderate leverage and no notable promoter pledges. Birlasoft has had CEO churn and the group has faced questions on sub-scale businesses (Orient Paper), but not on value transfers. Confidence: single-source for most items beyond the Orient Cement deal; verify SAST pledges and RPT notes before relying.

data.good_conduct: Orient Cement exit with open offer at same price
